item_description: The Japanese sun kami and a central figure in Shinto tradition.
item_facts: Amaterasu appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki chronicles.
She is associated with the imperial myth of descent through Ninigi.
Her stories are part of living religious tradition, not only ancient mythology.
needs_review: Verify narrative details against translated primary texts and Japanese scholarship.

item_description: A trickster figure in Akan and other West African storytelling traditions, often appearing as a spider or person.
item_facts: Anansi stories spread through the African diaspora, including the Caribbean.
Tales often use wit and cleverness to challenge more powerful characters.
Versions vary across communities and oral traditions.
needs_review: Treat as a living and diverse oral tradition; verify cultural context with specialist sources.

item_description: A Greek goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare, also included among the Olympian deities.
item_facts: Athena was the patron goddess of Athens.
She is associated with the owl and the olive tree.
Greek stories describe her as emerging from Zeus’s head.
needs_review: Verify myth details and cultural context against ancient sources.

item_description: A Mexica deity associated with the sun and war, central to the religious traditions of Tenochtitlan.
item_facts: Huitzilopochtli was the patron deity of the Mexica (Aztec) people.
The Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan was dedicated jointly to him and Tlaloc.
Descriptions come from Indigenous and colonial-era sources that must be read critically.
needs_review: Use culturally informed scholarship and distinguish Mexica traditions from colonial accounts.

item_description: The sun deity of the Inca state religion and an important figure in Andean traditions.
item_facts: Inti was closely associated with Inca rulers and state ritual.
The Coricancha in Cusco was a major temple associated with the sun.
Knowledge of Inca religion comes partly through colonial-era accounts.
needs_review: Verify descriptions through Andean scholarship and account for colonial source bias.

item_description: A feathered serpent deity in Maya traditions, especially associated with the Yucatec Maya.
item_facts: Kukulkan is related by name and attributes to other Mesoamerican feathered serpent traditions.
The name is Yucatec Maya; Quetzalcoatl is a related Nahuatl name from central Mexico.
The famous pyramid at Chichén Itzá is associated with Kukulkan in modern interpretation.
needs_review: Avoid conflating Maya and Mexica traditions; verify archaeological interpretations.

item_description: A chief god of ancient Babylon who became central to Babylonian state religion.
item_facts: Marduk is the central divine figure in the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish.
The epic describes his rise to supremacy among the gods.
His principal temple complex was Esagila in Babylon.
needs_review: Verify text interpretation, dates and temple history using Assyriological sources.

item_description: A Chinese sea goddess revered by seafarers and coastal communities, especially in southern China and Taiwan.
item_facts: Mazu worship developed around the historical figure Lin Moniang in later tradition.
Her cult spread through maritime communities across East and Southeast Asia.
Mazu remains an important figure in living religious practice.
needs_review: Historical personhood and biography are shaped by devotional tradition; verify with cultural sources.

item_description: A major god in Norse sources, associated with wisdom, poetry, war and the dead.
item_facts: Odin is a central figure in the Poetic Edda and Prose Edda.
He is associated with ravens named Huginn and Muninn.
Norse religious practice and medieval literary portrayals are not identical.
needs_review: Distinguish medieval textual accounts from historical pre-Christian practices.

item_description: A Slavic thunder god known from historical and folkloric traditions across Slavic regions.
item_facts: Perun is often associated with thunder, lightning and oak trees.
He appears in medieval accounts of East Slavic religion.
Details vary across Slavic cultures and later folklore.
needs_review: Evidence is fragmentary and regionally varied; verify reconstructions through specialist scholarship.

item_description: The Greek god of the sea, earthquakes and horses in ancient Greek religion and literature.
item_facts: Poseidon is a brother of Zeus and Hades in Greek myth.
His symbols include a trident.
The Roman deity Neptune shares some associations but belongs to a distinct religious tradition.
needs_review: Verify ancient contexts and avoid treating Greek and Roman traditions as identical.

item_description: A feathered serpent deity known from central Mexican traditions, with forms and meanings that changed across cultures and eras.
item_facts: The name is Nahuatl and is commonly translated as 'feathered serpent.'
Quetzalcoatl was associated with wind and learning in some traditions.
The deity should not be collapsed into the distinct Maya figure Kukulkan.
needs_review: Verify historical interpretations and avoid modernized or colonial simplifications.

item_description: An ancient Egyptian sun deity whose identity was combined with other gods in different periods.
item_facts: Ra was associated with the sun and kingship.
He was often shown with a falcon head and sun disk.
Amun-Ra and Ra-Horakhty are examples of combined divine forms.
needs_review: Verify period-specific forms and iconography using Egyptological sources.

item_description: A major Hindu deity revered in Shaiva traditions and associated with transformation and cosmic cycles.
item_facts: Shiva is one of the most widely worshipped deities in Hinduism.
He is often depicted with a trident and a crescent moon.
His theological meanings vary across Hindu traditions.
needs_review: Respect living religious context and verify descriptions across traditions.

item_description: A Māori atua associated with forests and birds in Māori cosmological traditions.
item_facts: In a widely told creation narrative, Tāne separates Ranginui and Papatūānuku.
Tāne is associated with forests and living things.
Māori iwi and traditions preserve distinct versions and interpretations.
needs_review: Use correct macrons and iwi-specific context; verify with Māori cultural sources.

item_description: A prominent figure in medieval Irish mythological literature, associated with abundance and leadership among the Tuatha Dé Danann.
item_facts: The Dagda appears in the Mythological Cycle of Irish literature.
Stories associate him with a cauldron, a club and a harp.
These accounts were recorded in medieval Christian manuscripts, not contemporary pagan sources.
needs_review: Distinguish medieval literary evidence from claims about pre-Christian religion.

item_description: A Norse thunder god known from medieval Scandinavian sources and later popular culture.
item_facts: Thor is associated with the hammer Mjölnir.
He appears in the Poetic Edda and Prose Edda.
The Marvel character is a modern fictional adaptation, not a direct account of Norse religion.
needs_review: Separate historical source material from later adaptations and verify details against translations.

item_description: A central rain and storm deity in Mexica and other Mesoamerican traditions.
item_facts: Tlaloc was worshipped at the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan.
He is associated with rain, fertility and agricultural cycles.
His forms and worship predate and extend beyond the Mexica empire.
needs_review: Verify Mesoamerican scope and historical continuity through specialist sources.

item_description: A principal Hindu deity worshipped especially in Vaishnava traditions and associated with preserving cosmic order.
item_facts: Vishnu is linked with avatars such as Rama and Krishna in many traditions.
He is commonly depicted holding a conch, discus, mace and lotus.
Different Hindu schools interpret Vishnu’s relationship to other deities differently.
needs_review: Represent theological diversity and verify claims with tradition-specific context.

item_description: The king of the Olympian gods in Greek mythology, associated with the sky, thunder and authority.
item_facts: Zeus is a son of Cronus and Rhea in Greek genealogies.
He is associated with Mount Olympus in many literary sources.
His cult titles and roles differed among ancient Greek communities.
needs_review: Verify literary and cult details against primary classical sources.
